# Escalation matrix

A severity-by-severity response plan — definition, response target, escalation trigger, and a named first responder — honestly flagging any severity nobody's actually assigned to yet.

Family: Daily management · Format: .xlsx · Domain: core

## What it is

An escalation matrix answers, for each severity level, three questions before something goes wrong: what qualifies as this severity, how fast should it be acknowledged, and when does it escalate further? Describe the severities this process needs, and a real matrix gets drafted — but who specifically responds is never guessed. Every row starts unassigned until you name a real person.

## When to use it

Use it when:

- A process handles issues of genuinely different urgency and you want a real, checkable plan for each level, not an ad hoc judgment call every time.
- You want to catch a severity with nobody actually assigned before it matters, not during a real incident.
- You want response targets and escalation triggers specific enough to actually check against, not vague aspirations.

Not when:

- Every issue in this process is genuinely the same urgency — a matrix with one row adds process without adding clarity.
- You don't have a real person to name yet — that's fine, the matrix will honestly show the gap; don't invent a name to make it look complete.

## How to fill it in

- **rows** — Drafted from your severities — assign a real, named first responder to each row.
- **narrative** — Drafted from the matrix actually built.

## What good looks like

The example below is the renewal-risk support process's own escalation matrix. Three of four severities have a named first responder — Critical and High route to specific people, Low routes to the standing rotation — and Medium is honestly left unassigned rather than padded with a placeholder name.

Full worked example, on-screen and as a downloadable .xlsx: https://katafacts.com/katas/escalation-matrix

## Common mistakes

- **Writing a response target like 'quickly' or 'as soon as possible.'** — An unchecked target can't actually be checked — a real matrix needs a real number, even a rough one, or it can't tell you when something's slipping.
- **Naming a placeholder responder just to make every row look assigned.** — A matrix with a fake name is worse than an honestly unassigned row — it hides exactly the gap the matrix exists to surface.
- **Building the matrix once and never checking it against how issues are actually handled.** — An escalation matrix nobody follows in practice isn't a real plan — revisit it when the real pattern of issues doesn't match what's on paper.

## What it connects to

Upstream:

- **Leader standard work** — Walking the queue against the escalation matrix — not just gut feel — is a natural leader standard work step.

## Where AI helps

Judgement — stays with you:

- Deciding who's actually the right first responder for a given severity
- Deciding whether a drafted response target is realistic given real team capacity

Analysis — AI helps:

- Drafting a specific severity definition, response target, and escalation trigger from a rough description
- Drafting the narrative from the matrix actually built

Drudgery — automated:

- Counting how many severities have a named responder
- Identifying which severities are still unassigned
- Exporting to xlsx in the house format
